input:
Basis

This report presents the design of an amine absorber which has been developed in order to remove the key component from a gas stream by means of absorption into an amine solution. The design throughput of the unit is 10 t per day, and the removal duty that the design is required to achieve is 98% of the key component present in the feed gas. The feed gas has been taken exactly as it is received at the battery limit, with the composition and the state declared by the upstream unit, and the absorber has been designed for continuous operation at the duty stated above. The solvent is an aqueous amine solution which is circulated between the absorber and a regeneration step that falls outside the scope of the present report. The scope of the design itself covers the column shell, the packing together with its supports, the liquid distributors, the sump, and the nozzles located at the battery limit. All wetted parts are fabricated in 316L stainless steel, which is stated here once, as the material basis on which the whole of this report rests. The design pressure and the design temperature correspond to the highest pressure and temperature that the column can be expected to meet in service, each of them carrying the margin that is required by the applicable code, and the relief case is determined by the blocked outlet of the gas stream. The solvent circulation rate, the lean loading and the rich loading are design variables which are fixed by the sizing, within the working limits stated by the solvent supplier for the solution that is in use. It should be noted that no credit has been taken in the basis for operating experience gained on other units, and that no performance figure beyond the stated removal duty is claimed for the column as it has been designed.

Sizing

The diameter of the column is established by the gas rate at the design throughput and by the phenomenon of flooding within the packing. The diameter has been selected in such a way that the design gas rate stands below the flooding rate by the margin that the packing correlation requires if stable operation is to be achieved, with the liquid rate held at its design value within the same check. The height of packing is established by the transfer calculation corresponding to the stated removal duty: the number of transfer units is derived from the separation that the duty demands, and the height of a transfer unit is derived from the performance of the packing at the design gas and liquid rates, so that the height overall is a consequence of the duty rather than a round figure that has been chosen in advance. The liquid is distributed by means of a distributor which is rated for the design liquid rate across the whole of the column section, and a redistributor is provided wherever the packed height is divided into more than one bed. The sump is sized to hold the solvent inventory that the circulation loop requires for stable level control, and the gas outlet is fitted with a demister in order to keep the carry-over of solvent into the treated gas within the limit that the downstream unit is able to accept. The sizes of the nozzles follow the usual velocity practice for the service at each of the connections. It is important to emphasise that the sizing is stated for the design case only; operation at rates that differ from the design case has not been sized here, and is instead carried forward as an open item into the risks section.

Materials

All wetted parts are manufactured in the stainless steel grade that is named in the basis, and this grade is used for the shell, for the packing, for the distributors, for the internals of the sump and for the wetted necks of the nozzles. The selection has been made on the basis of the corrosion behaviour that is characteristic of amine service: it is the rich solution, loaded with the component that has been absorbed, that acts as the corrodent within the column, and its attack is at its strongest in those locations where the solution is at its hottest and where its velocity is at its highest. The degradation products of the amine themselves add to the corrosivity of the circulating solution, and this forms part of the reasoning behind the selection of a stainless grade for the wetted parts, rather than carbon steel. Welds that are exposed to the wetted service are made with a filler of matching composition, and crevices have been kept out of the wetted design wherever a crevice would tend to hold rich solution against a surface. Parts that are not wetted, which include the skirt and the external attachments, are made of carbon steel with a protective coating that is suitable for the atmosphere of the site. The gaskets at the wetted joints have been selected for their resistance to the amine solution at the design temperature. Access for inspection is provided at the sump and at each bed, so that the wetted surfaces on which the corrosion argument depends can be examined during service outages.

Risks

There are two significant open items that are addressed in this section, namely fouling and turndown, and it should be clearly understood that neither of these items is resolved in this report. Fouling in amine service arises from the degradation solids that are present in the circulating solution and from carry-over that enters the column together with the feed gas; the first effect that it produces in the absorber is a rise in the pressure drop across the packing, which is followed by maldistribution of the liquid and by a fall in the removal that the column is able to achieve. No fouling rate has been included in the design, because no rate obtained from a comparable duty is available to this report, and the provision that is made for monitoring is a trended measurement of the pressure drop across the packed beds, which is read against the clean condition that will be recorded at commissioning. What is missing at this stage is a fouling allowance: until such time as a rate has been established, neither the cleaning interval nor the margin in the packed height can properly be settled. Turndown remains open for a corresponding reason. At gas rates below the design case, the distribution of the liquid and the wetting of the packing both fall away, and the removal duty is placed at risk before any limit in the packing itself is actually reached; the lowest gas rate at which the stated duty still holds has not yet been established, either by testing or by vendor evidence, for the packing that has been selected. Both of these items are therefore carried forward into detailed design as open items, with the design as stated standing on the design case alone.

Basis

The design throughput is 10 t per day, and the removal duty is 98% of the key component in the feed gas. No credit is taken in the basis for operating experience on other units, and no performance figure beyond the stated removal duty is claimed for the column as designed. The treated gas leaves the column to the downstream unit named in the battery limits, and the rich solution leaves the sump to regeneration; neither stream is treated further in this report. The basis also records that the feed, as declared by the upstream unit, contains no component that the solvent cannot tolerate at the stated duty.

Sizing

The column diameter is set by the gas rate at the design throughput and by flooding in the packing. The diameter is chosen so that the design gas rate stands below the flooding rate by the margin the packing correlation requires for stable operation, with the liquid rate at its design value in the same check. Nozzle sizes follow the velocity practice for the service at each connection. The pressure drop across the packing at the design case is calculated from the packing correlation at the design gas and liquid rates, and is held within the allowance the gas stream can meet at the battery limit. Internals clearances and the packing support grid follow the packing vendor's standard arrangement for the diameter chosen, and the bed arrangement keeps each bed shallow enough for the redistributor to restore an even liquid spread across the section. The sizing is stated at the design case only; operation at rates away from the design case is not sized here and is carried as an open item in the risks section.

Materials

Wetted parts are the stainless steel grade named in the basis, and that grade is used for the shell, the packing, the distributors, the sump internals and the wetted nozzle necks. Inspection access is provided at the sump and at each bed, so that the wetted surfaces the corrosion argument depends on can be examined in service outages. Bolting at wetted flanges follows the wetted selection where the joint is opened in service, and small-bore connections in wetted service are of the same grade as the parts they attach to, so that no wetted surface in the column falls below the basis selection.

Risks

Fouling and turndown are open items, and neither is resolved in this report. Fouling in amine service arises from degradation solids in the circulating solution and from carry-over into the column with the feed gas; its first effect in the absorber is a rise in pressure drop across the packing, followed by maldistribution of the liquid and a fall in the removal the column achieves. Each open item is stated with the evidence that would close it, so that detailed design can take the items in the order in which their evidence arrives. Both items are carried into detailed design as open items, with the design as stated standing on the design case alone.
